scenes.title: Three Kinds of Hearer, Three Kinds of Speech
scenes.summary: A speech has a speaker, a subject and a hearer, and its end is directed at the hearer, who is either a spectator or a judge of past or future things. So there are three kinds of rhetoric: deliberative, judicial and epideictic.

scenes.title: Their Parts and Their Times
scenes.summary: Deliberation exhorts or dissuades and looks to the future; a lawsuit accuses or defends and looks to the past; epideictic praises or blames and looks chiefly to the present, though it recalls the past and forecasts the future.

scenes.title: Their Ends
scenes.summary: The adviser's end is the advantageous and the harmful, the litigant's the just and the unjust, the epideictic speaker's the noble and the shameful; each brings in the others in support. A sign: litigants may admit an act but never the wrong, advisers ignore injustice to neighbors, and praise honors Achilles for helping Patroclus knowing he must die.

scenes.title: The Common Premises
scenes.summary: All three kinds need premises from tekmēria, probabilities and signs; premises about the possible and the impossible, about whether a thing happened or will happen; and premises about greatness and smallness, the greater and the lesser good or wrong. Each kind's own subjects come next.
